title: Spaced Repetition
tags: [learning, productivity, anki, memory]
date: 2025-04-05
---

I spent most of last Sunday afternoon reorganizing my Anki decks again. The living room was a mess with my laptop on the coffee table, a cold cup of coffee next to it, and the cat trying to walk across the keyboard every ten minutes. It feels like every few months I end up tweaking my spaced repetition settings because something no longer feels quite right. 

Spaced repetition is one of those techniques that sounds almost too simple when you first hear about it. The basic idea is that you review information at increasing intervals of time, just before you are likely to forget it. This strengthens the memory trace each time. I first came across the concept while reading about [[Learning]] strategies last year and it completely changed how I approach retaining new information.

The core of my current system lives in Anki. After a lot of trial and error I have settled on some specific parameters that seem to work well for me. My learning steps are set to **1m 10m**. This means when I first see a new card I have one minute to rate it, then ten minutes later it comes back again if I got it right. It gives just enough time for the information to start settling without overwhelming me with immediate reviews.

Once a card graduates from the learning stage, the initial graduating interval is **3 days**. I used to have this set to one day but found I was seeing the same cards too frequently and it created review fatigue. Three days feels like the sweet spot. It gives the memory some time to fade just enough that retrieving it requires real effort, which is apparently key to strengthening it.

One mistake I made early on was setting the maximum number of new cards per day to 50. That number sounded reasonable when I read it in some popular Anki guides, but in practice it was way too many for me. I would get through the new cards but then the review burden would snowball over the following week. After several frustrating months I finally reduced it to **20 new cards a day**. That feels much more sustainable. Some days I even lower it further to 10 or 15 if I know my week is going to be busy.

The long-term intervals seem to be working nicely now. I have been adding cards from my [[Learning]] notes about cognitive science, philosophy, and even some language vocabulary. The beauty of spaced repetition is that it handles the scheduling automatically. I just have to show up and do the reviews honestly.

There are still days when I sit down with Anki and feel a bit resistant. Twenty new cards does not sound like much until you have been doing it consistently for months and your review queue starts creeping up toward 200 cards. On those days I remind myself that the whole point is to make the information stick without having to cram. I usually put on some instrumental music, make a fresh cup of tea, and just chip away at it.

I have also been experimenting with how I write the cards themselves. The more specific and atomic I can make the questions, the better the retention seems to be. Vague cards tend to get leeched or suspended eventually. There is definitely an art to it.

Overall I am pretty happy with where my spaced repetition practice is at the moment. The combination of 1m 10m learning steps, 3 day graduating interval, and a strict limit of 20 new cards daily has created a rhythm that feels manageable. I still have plenty to learn about optimizing the system further, but for now this setup is letting me actually retain the things I am studying instead of just cycling through them and forgetting.

Tomorrow I will probably review the notes I took during that [[Learning]] seminar last month and turn a few key insights into new cards. Slow and steady seems to be the way forward.
